newsitem.title: USA: Dlr off at US noon, stung by mark surge in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr off at US noon, stung by mark surge in Europe.

text.p: The dollar was smarting at noon, hurt as the mark jumped in Europe after a poll showed French voters want a referendum on monetary union, fearing it would threaten jobs and economic growth, dealers said.

After a couple of stabs at the 1.72-mark area on Thursday, the dollar eased below 1.7150, as the mark firmed against the French franc in the wake of the survey released by the Louis Harris institute for Valeurs Actuelles magazine.
"There is continued resistance up at 1.7200 marks. Europe tried it, we tried it, but there seems to be selling up there," said Ben Strauss, of Bank Julius Baer and Co.
"The main reason is the firmer tone in the European Monetary System on the back of the French poll," Strauss, an assistant vice president for foreign exchange, continued.
Of those polled, 69 percent favored a new referendum on the euro. French voters narrowly approved the Maastricht Treaty on European Economic and Monetary Union in a 1992 referendum.
The mark probed the 3.3750 French level in midmorning U.S. trade. It also rose against the lira and other EMS units.
Dollar/mark fell to 1.7150/60 at midday, from 1.7185/95 at the open. The dollar eased to 125.90/00 yen from 126.08/18.

The Harris poll also showed most French citizens believed there were alternatives to the center-right government's economic policies aimed at securing entry to EMU in 1999. France is preparing for elections on May 25 and June 1.

Indeed, rumors that another poll indicated the current conservative majority in the National Assembly might be shaved to just three seats, leaving its EMU plans hanging by a thread, also weighed on the franc.
"That seems to be weakening the French from here," said Susan Stearns, a director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal. "The specter of further referenda is not good."
The dollar moved lower in an orderly fashion, remaining well above its overnight low of 1.7108 marks. A dearth of economic data limited activity.

Caution ahead of Friday's meeting between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also deadened trade. But the big event remains Sunday's gathering of central bankers and finance ministers from the seven big industrial powers, dealers said.
"Ahead of the G7 I don't think the market is willing to do anything," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president at Credit Agricole.
Flanagan said there is a growing perception that the G7 will not produce a much stronger statement to curb the dollar's recent strength than it issued after the last confab in Berlin.
At that meeting in February the G7 said currencies had corrected from misalignments in early 1995, when the dollar was near record lows, and that forex stability was desirable.
While G7 policymakers may voice their concern about a rapidly rising dollar this weekend, they will probably stop short of any overt shift in exchange rate policy this time, currency experts said.
Traders said dollar/yen was capped by offers from Japanese banks near 126.35. The dollar ducked under 126 yen, where importers were earlier said to have had interest to purchase.
Mark/yen was propped above its early Thursday low near 73.30 during the U.S. morning session.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4610/20 Swiss francs from 1.4660/70. It rose to Canadian $1.3923/28 from C$1.3913/18.
The pound rose to $1.6248/58 from $1.6225/30.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
